title: Definition of the Differentiated Services Field (DS Field) in the IPv4 and IPv6 Headers
subtitle: Six bits in the IP header that tell every router how to treat a packet.
summary: RFC 2474 redefines the old IPv4 Type of Service octet and the IPv6 Traffic Class octet as the Differentiated Services (DS) field. Six of its eight bits form the DS codepoint (DSCP), which a router maps to a per-hop behavior such as best effort or priority queueing; the other two bits are left unused. It keeps partial compatibility with IP Precedence through eight Class Selector codepoints.

eli5.summary: Every parcel gets a colored sticker on the outside. Postal workers do not open the parcel; they just look at the sticker and decide which pile it goes in, fast or slow.

questions: what is the ds field in the ip header
how does diffserv relate to ip precedence
what happened to the ipv4 tos byte

tldr.problem: The IPv4 TOS octet and IPv6 Traffic Class octet had no agreed, scalable meaning for giving some packets better treatment than others.
tldr.mechanism: The first six bits of that octet become the DSCP, which each router maps through a configurable table to a per-hop behavior; the last two bits are currently unused.
tldr.outcome: Networks mark traffic once at their edge and interior routers just read the codepoint, so differentiated service scales without per-flow state in the core.

today: The DS field is in nearly every IP packet. Operators mark traffic such as voice, video or network control at the network edge, and routers and switches queue by DSCP. Later documents defined the actual PHBs and codepoints (for example Assured Forwarding and Expedited Forwarding), and RFC 8436 later changed how Pool 3 codepoints are registered with IANA. The two low bits are now used for Explicit Congestion Notification, defined in RFC 3168.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Differentiated services aims to give the Internet scalable service discrimination. The authors split the problem the same way the Internet splits forwarding from routing. The forwarding path, where each packet is treated according to a mark in its header, is well understood and can be standardised now. The policy and allocation side, which decides who gets what, is still evolving and is deliberately left out.

This RFC therefore covers only the forwarding path: a field in the IP header holds a codepoint, and each node maps that codepoint to a per-hop behavior (PHB), implemented with queue service or queue management such as weighted round-robin or drop preference. Marking is done by traffic conditioners at network boundaries.

It is meant to be read with the architecture document, RFC 2475, and it states plainly that it is a concise description of the DS field and its uses.
sections.eli5: Think of a mail sorting room. Deciding the rules for who deserves fast delivery is a complicated business question. This document only says where the sticker goes and what the workers do when they see it.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
Section 2 defines the vocabulary used throughout. A codepoint is a specific value of the DSCP portion of the field. A behavior aggregate is all the packets with the same codepoint crossing a link in one direction. A per-hop behavior is the externally observable forwarding treatment a compliant node gives an aggregate, and a PHB group is a set of PHBs that only make sense specified together.

A DS domain is a contiguous part of the Internet run with one consistent set of policies, and its edge is the DS boundary, where classifiers and traffic conditioners (meters, markers, shapers, policers) usually sit. A microflow is one application-to-application flow identified by addresses, protocol and ports.

The RFC defines the DS field as the IPv4 TOS octet or the IPv6 Traffic Class octet "when interpreted in conformance with" this document. It is the same byte on the wire, read differently.
sections.eli5: A neighborhood with the same rules for mail is a domain. The sticker is the codepoint, and the way the sorters treat that sticker is the behavior.

sections.title: The DS Field
sections.content:
The DS field is a replacement for the IPv4 TOS octet from RFC 791 and the IPv6 Traffic Class octet from RFC 2460. Six bits are the DSCP, used to select the PHB at each node. The remaining two bits are the CU (currently unused) field, whose definition is out of scope, and DS-compliant nodes must ignore them when choosing a PHB.

Written as 'xxxxxx', the left-most bit is bit 0 of the DS field. Nodes must select PHBs by matching the entire 6-bit DSCP, for example by using it as an index into a table, and the DSCP is defined as an unstructured field to allow future PHBs.

Configurable mapping
A node must support the logical equivalent of a configurable table from codepoints to PHBs, with exceptions for 'xxx000'.
Unknown codepoints
Packets with an unrecognised codepoint should be forwarded as Default and their codepoints not changed.
Rewriting
Nodes may rewrite the DS field to provide a local or end-to-end service.
sections.eli5: The sticker has eight little squares. The first six say which pile to use. The last two are blank for now, and the workers ignore them.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
The new layout is incompatible with the old TOS octet, whose bits were Precedence, then delay, throughput and reliability flags. The RFC makes no attempt to keep the "DTR" bits, but it does keep a limited compatibility with the three-bit IP Precedence field in bits 0-2, which routers were already using to choose queues.

It does this in two steps. First, a Default PHB must exist in every node: ordinary best-effort forwarding, recommended codepoint '000000', and it is not configurable. Unmapped codepoints should map to it. Second, the eight Class Selector codepoints 'xxx000' must map to PHBs that meet the Class Selector requirements: at least two independently forwarded classes, a higher-valued selector should not get a lower probability of timely forwarding, and '11x000' must be treated better than '000000' so routing traffic keeps working.

Because mappings are configurable, an operator can ignore bits 3-5, so '011010' behaves like '011000' and old Precedence-style networks keep working.
sections.eli5: Some post offices already used the first three squares of the old sticker. So the new system keeps those eight piles working the way they did, plus a normal pile that everything falls into if nobody says otherwise.

sections.title: PHB Standardization Guidelines
sections.content:
The RFC standardises behaviors, not mechanisms. A vendor may use strict priority, weighted fair queueing, weighted round-robin or class-based queueing, as long as the externally visible behavior matches the PHB definition. This keeps the standard stable while queueing algorithms evolve.

PHBs may be specified singly or as a group. A group specification should describe when a packet might be re-marked to another PHB in the group, and must identify any packet re-ordering that could happen inside a microflow. PHB implementations are recommended not to re-order packets within a microflow.

Only PHBs that are not already covered, and that have been implemented, deployed and shown useful, should be standardised, and each standardised PHB must have a recommended codepoint. The defined space 'xxx000' is intentionally sparse to leave room for growth. Specifications are recommended to follow the guidelines in RFC 2475.
sections.eli5: The rule book says what has to happen to a parcel with a given sticker, not how the sorting machine is built. Any machine that gives the right result is fine.

sections.title: Codepoint Space and IANA
sections.content:
A six-bit DSCP carries 64 codepoints, divided into three pools. Pool 1 holds 32 codepoints of the form 'xxxxx0', assigned by Standards Action. Pool 2 holds 16 of the form 'xxxx11' for experimental or local use (EXP/LU). Pool 3 holds 16 of the form 'xxxx01', also for experimental or local use at first, but available for standardised assignments if Pool 1 runs out.

This document itself assigns only the eight Class Selector codepoints 'xxx000' from Pool 1. They are mapped not to specific PHBs but to PHBs that meet "at least" the Class Selector requirements.

RFC 8436 later updated this RFC by changing the IANA registration procedure for Pool 3 values.
sections.eli5: There are 64 possible stickers. Half are saved for official use, and the rest are for tests or for each post office to use however it wants.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because better treatment is chosen by the codepoint, an attacker can steal service by setting a high-priority codepoint or injecting marked packets, and enough of it becomes a denial of service. The defense is conditioning at DS boundaries: boundary nodes must make sure all traffic entering the domain is marked appropriately, re-marking if necessary. Interior nodes trust the codepoint and are not required to check it.

IPsec complicates this. The DS field is not part of IPsec's cryptographic calculations (for tunnel mode, the outer header's field), so IPsec neither protects it nor is broken by changes to it. In tunnel mode the inner header's DS field is protected, and decapsulation must not change it. A tunnel egress that cannot trust the inner field must treat the packet as arriving from outside the domain; with a strong enough integrity check it can assume the value is unchanged.
sections.eli5: If anyone can write "rush" on their own parcel, the fast lane jams. So the post office checks stickers at the front door, and the workers inside trust them.
